headlines.title: Robot factories and hypersonic missiles: JPMorgan Chase's first $5 billion of defense investments
headlines.summary: With $5 billion already deployed off its balance sheet, JPMorgan Chase is racing ahead on direct investments in defense tech, hardware and supply chains.
headlines.article_text: JPMorgan's $5 billion bet on U.S. security; startups Castelion, Hadrian Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points JPMorgan Chase has deployed $5 billion into startup investments in the first year of its U.S. security and resiliency initiative, halfway to its initial $10 billion goal. The bank may exceed that target, co-President Doug Petno told CNBC. JPMorgan has taken stakes in startups Hadrian, which builds automated factories for aerospace and defense firms, and Castelion, which is developing low-cost hypersonic missiles. Separately, JPMorgan has financed and facilitated more than $230 billion in transactions in the initiative's first year, part of a broader goal of supporting $1.5 trillion in activity over a decade. In this article JPM Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT The head of JPMorgan's new security and resiliency initiative, Todd Combs, then portfolio manager at Berkshire Hathaway Inc., is seen at Berkshire Hathaway's shareholders meeting in Omaha, Nebraska, May 4, 2014. Daniel Acker / Bloomberg / Getty Images JPMorgan Chase has made $5 billion in startup investments in the first year of its U.S. security and resiliency initiative , the company said Monday, a faster-than-expected pace that indicates the bank is finding plentiful opportunities in emerging defense, manufacturing and supply chain firms. The bank, which last year said it would deploy $10 billion into startups over a decade, may expand the program beyond that initial dollar amount, JPMorgan co-President Doug Petno told CNBC in an interview. Todd Combs, the former Berkshire Hathaway executive who leads the JPMorgan group in charge of making startup investments , has "hit the ground running," Petno said. "He's done a great job and put us in some really interesting companies," he added. Most of those investments have yet to be disclosed, but two known stakes seem emblematic of the project's mission to bolster companies that are needed for a more dangerous and chaotic era of geopolitics. JPMorgan, the biggest U.S. bank by assets, has taken direct stakes in defense-related startups Hadrian and Castelion . Wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, as well as trade disputes with China, have threatened the flow of energy and key components needed for U.S. industries and defense, which spurred JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon into creating the initiative a year ago. He put Petno, widely seen as one of two key possible successors , in charge of the overall investment project. Combs, a former board member of the bank, reports directly to Dimon. The scope of the project extends beyond supply chain, defense and manufacturing to include frontier technologies and the pharmaceutical and health-tech industries. Troy Rohrbaugh and Douglas Petno, co-CEOs of Commercial & Investment Bank at JPMorganChase. Courtesy: JPMorganChase "There's a lot of really interesting companies that have been working to solve some of these problems," Petno said. These "early venture-stage, advanced manufacturing companies have found ways to build these capabilities in the U.S." rather than relying on overseas trading partners, he said. In August, the bank helped lead a $1.4 billion funding round for Hadrian, which builds automated factories that make parts for the defense, aerospace and maritime sectors. A California factory run by Hadrian has 10 robots for every human employee, according to the startup's founder. That month, JPMorgan was also involved in a $1 billion funding round for Castelion, whose flagship product is a relatively low-cost hypersonic missile called Blackbeard. Castelion was founded in late 2022 by a group of former SpaceX engineers. "Our approach is to find generational companies and partner with them for the long term," Combs said in a statement Monday. "Putting more than $5 billion to work in our first year shows how many exceptional businesses are building in industries that strengthen critical supply chains," Combs said. Risky business? JPMorgan making billions of dollars of direct investments in nascent companies is a departure from its usual role as a lender and advisor. Before the defense initiative, the bank had moved away from taking startup stakes, which can be relatively risky bets on unproven technologies. JPMorgan spun off its private equity business, One Equity Partners, more than a decade ago. In its more traditional role, JPMorgan has also financed and facilitated more than $230 billion for industries that support American national interests, according to the bank. That part of its security and resiliency project, meant to hit $1.5 trillion over 10 years, is led by Jay Horine , a former co-head of investment banking. JPMorgan built a team for the project of about three dozen bankers, who are aided by hundreds more across the firm, as it expanded the initiative to Europe and Canada. Its bankers are mapping distribution lines for key products, from submarines and missiles to aircraft, to identify suppliers that may lack the capital or capacity to meet rising demand, according to Petno. In this article SPCX Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 3:00 03:00 Elon Musk to give away one SpaceX share to every American child next year Squawk Box Europe SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said Monday that he'll give every child in the U.S. one of his shares in the company next year. Musk currently owns about 4.8 billion SpaceX shares, according to an August SEC filing. That figure rises to 6.4 billion when taking into account unvested awards and stock options, representing a 48.4% beneficial stake in the company. There were 72 million children under 18 in the U.S. as of July 1, 2025, according to official census data. That would amount to the CEO giving away about $10.5 billion worth of shares, taking into account SpaceX's closing stock price of $146.03 as of Friday. "This will be the first of many," Musk said in a post on X, without providing further details on how the share giveaway would happen. CNBC has reached out to SpaceX for further comment. Musk's financial giving has been in the news in recent weeks primarily for his political contributions. The Tesla CEO has spent more than $276 million in donations to Republican groups since July, making him the biggest known donor of the 2026 midterm election. The world's richest person poured $158 million into the Senate Leadership Fund, the Republican Party's leading Senate super PAC, in September through an affiliated Texas PAC created to support Republican Ken Paxton. Musk's two contributions of $75 million and $83 million are among the largest political donations ever. Musk's post came hot on the heels of Anthropic revealing that it plans to commit 5% of its shares to a new public benefit fund, with the stake potentially increasing as the company's valuation grows. In response to an Anthropic post on X about the fund on Sunday, Musk replied, "I recommend giving the shares directly to the public," and added that's what he'd be doing. Subject to shareholder approval, Anthropic's fund would immediately commit 5% of Anthropic's shares, with the board adding, at its discretion, an additional 2% for every 50% increase in the company's value above a set baseline that has yet to be disclosed. The fund may be used to "explore large donations," including to traditional nonprofits or as direct distributions for specific populations, or for "bolder approaches" to study and address AI's disruption and displacement of jobs, the company said. — CNBC's Jennifer Liu contributed to this report. headlines.title: Google says it can build data centers the right way. Some experts and residents are skeptical
headlines.summary: Google says its Minnesota AI data center will add clean energy to the grid and protect ratepayers. Experts question whether grid upgrades are needed.
headlines.article_text: How AI data centers are reshaping America's aging grid Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points AI data centers are poised to drive North America’s electricity demand growth over the next decade, fueling a massive grid buildout. Google and Xcel Energy say their proposed 780-megawatt data center in Minnesota will upgrade the grid with cleaner power without shifting infrastructure costs onto existing customers. But experts say much of that buildout could be avoided and warn that utilities have a financial incentive to keep building. In this article GOOGL SPCX XEL Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 11:44 11:44 The race to power AI data centers is reshaping America's electric grid Tech If there's one thing most Americans can agree on, it's that they don't want a data center in their backyard. A Gallup survey conducted in March found that 71% of Americans opposed the construction of a data center in their local area. Chief among their concerns: energy usage. Half of Americans surveyed by Pew Research Center in July and August said data centers would be mostly bad for the environment and for household energy costs. Now Google is betting that a massive AI data center can help finance a cleaner, more reliable power grid. Its proposed deal with Xcel Energy would add more wind, solar and battery capacity than the data center is expected to use. Under the agreement, Google would help pay for the added capacity and continue paying, even if it doesn't use all of the power. Google's bet that AI can finance a cleaner grid Pine Island, Minnesota, is a small town of about 4,000 residents an hour southeast of Minneapolis. Google hopes that its new 780-megawatt data center plan will build goodwill with the Pine Island community and keep the company on track to meet its goal of operating on carbon-free energy, 24 hours a day, seven days a week by 2030 . Google — whose cloud business powers its own Gemini AI and brought in nearly $25 billion in second-quarter revenue, an 82% increase from a year earlier — says it has found a model for doing this the right way. The company plans to finance the addition of 1,400 megawatts of wind, 200 megawatts of solar and 300 megawatts of battery storage to Xcel's grid. Those additions amount to more than the capacity of the data center itself, which Google said is because wind and solar do not generate energy at all times. Xcel Energy said the new power will serve all customers in the local area, not just Google. Xcel also said the upgrades will help advance the local grid's carbon-free energy supply. The proposed agreement between Google and Xcel includes minimum demand charges and exit fees, which Google says will keep the company on the hook for the infrastructure being built on its behalf, even if the AI boom cools. Google will pay for at least 75% of its contracted capacity, even if it uses less, and would owe up to eight years' worth of those minimum demand charges if it terminates the agreement early. "Nobody wants to have a big buildout and then have nowhere for that power to go and nobody to pay for that power," said Amanda Rome, executive vice president and chief customer officer at Xcel Energy. "That's where these protections come in." The agreement between Google and Xcel Energy is pending approval by the Minnesota Public Utilities Commission. Data centers are driving a historic power buildout New data centers will account for "most" of the projected increase in electricity demand over the next decade, according to the North American Electric Reliability Corporation, a nonprofit regulator. The Department of Energy under President Joe Biden reported that more than 70% of U.S. transmission lines and power transformers were at least 25 years old and found that the cheapest ways of meeting future demand would require the nation's transmission system to more than double in size by 2050 . But hyperscalers argue that they can finance badly needed grid upgrades while also making the grid cleaner and more reliable. "The timing of this industrial revolution couldn't be more perfect," said Amanda Peterson Corio, Google's global head of energy and power. "It's right at the time when we needed capital to fix aging infrastructure in the United States." Could data centers use the grid as is? Jigar Shah, a partner at Multiplier, a consulting firm that helps clean energy startups go public, said data center operators could be constructing smaller facilities in places where the grid already has unused capacity. That would minimize the need to build — and pay for — new generation or transmission equipment. "If you fit the load growth that the data centers want into the existing grid, everybody's rates go down by a lot," said Shah. That's because the existing grid has enormous fixed costs from the infrastructure already in place: power plants, transmission lines, substations. If one new customer comes onto the grid and pays a large slice of that, everyone else's bills go down. "And so the question really is, why are people not doing these 25-megawatt data centers? Why are they doing 1,000-megawatt data centers? And it turns out people are just lazy," Shah said. "They're like, well, it's easier for me to contract one data center that's one gigawatt in size than figuring out how to do something on the order of 40 data centers that are 25 megawatts each." Industry watchdogs also warn of another reason that utilities often prefer to build new infrastructure, rather than make more use out of their existing grid. "When [utilities] build something new, they fund part of that investment with dollars from their investors on Wall Street, and they enjoy incredibly high, exorbitant returns on those investments, typically around 10%," said David Pomerantz, executive director at the Energy and Policy Institute, a utility watchdog agency. Building a data center that fits neatly into an existing grid provides little opportunity for a utility to make new money. What if a hyperscaler offers to pay for those grid investments? "One way to leverage data centers to lower people's bills is for data centers to provide that capital at much cheaper rates than the utility," said Pomerantz. "But that's a big problem for the utility. And this fight is actually already emerging." Still, Shah said, the Google/Xcel project in Minnesota is a good example of a data center project acting as a catalyst for newer, greener technology. "Google came in and said, well, here's a new way of doing things, using new technologies. How about we do it that way? And then that helps ratepayers. And the utility was like, yeah, that makes a lot of sense." headlines.title: Cormedix Announces FDA Acceptance for Priority Review of Supplemental NDA for Rezzayo® (Rezafungin) for Prophylaxis of Invasive Fungal Diseases
headlines.summary: PARSIPPANY, N.J., Oct. 19, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- CorMedix Therapeutics (Nasdaq: CRMD) today announced that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has accepted for filing the supplemental New Drug Application (sNDA) seeking approval of REZZAYO® (rezafungin for injection) for the prophylaxis of invasive fungal disease. The sNDA was submitted by Mundipharma, CorMedix’s global development partner, and the FDA has granted Priority Review with a Prescription Drug User Fee Act (PDUFA) target action date in Q1 2027. The sNDA is supported by the Phase III ReSPECT pivotal study, for which CorMedix announced positive topline results in April. ReSPECT evaluated the efficacy and safety of once weekly rezafungin (rezafungin acetate) compared with a standard antimicrobial regimen (SAR) for the prophylaxis of invasive fungal diseases in adults undergoing allogeneic HSCT. If REZZAYO is approved for this new indication, CorMedix is targeting to begin promotional efforts beginning in H2 2027.

headlines.summary: MONCTON, New Brunswick, Oct. 19, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Major Drilling Group International Inc. Any such purchases may occur from time to time and in aggregate up to 4,111,846 Common Shares (being approximately 5% of the issued and outstanding Common Shares of Major Drilling) over a 12-month period commencing on October 21, 2026 and terminating on October 20, 2027. As of October 7, 2026, Major Drilling had 82,236,936 Common Shares issued and outstanding.
